facts.languages: Vietnamese, plus Nùng, Tày and Sán Dìu in the hills
facts.bestTime: The first lunar month, for village festivals such as Lim (13th day)
facts.founded: A province since 1831; merged with Bắc Giang in 2025

sections.title: Geography
sections.text: The old region of Kinh Bắc spreads across the flat delta north-east of Hà Nội, crossed by the Đuống and Cầu rivers. The former Bắc Giang province adds rolling hills to the east: Lục Ngạn, famous for lychees, and the western slopes of the Yên Tử range.

sections.title: History
sections.text: Under Chinese rule, Luy Lâu was the capital of the province of Giao Chỉ and one of the first centres of Buddhism in the region. Lý Công Uẩn, who founded the Lý dynasty in 1009, was born in this region. In March 1884 the French captured the citadel of Bắc Ninh. Today the province is one of Vietnam's largest manufacturing centres.

sections.title: Culture
sections.text: Bắc Ninh is the home of quan họ, a style of call-and-response folk singing listed by UNESCO in 2009. The village of Đông Hồ still makes colourful woodblock prints for the new year, using natural colours on paper made from tree bark and coated with ground seashells.

etiquette: Cover your shoulders and knees, and take off your hat inside the halls.
Walk around the main altar quietly, and let worshippers go first.
If invited to listen to quan họ, sit quietly and applaud at the end of each pair of songs.

timeline.text: Luy Lâu, capital of the Chinese-ruled province of Giao Chỉ, is a centre of trade and early Buddhism.
Lý Công Uẩn, born in this region, becomes emperor and founds the Lý dynasty.
Dâu Pagoda is rebuilt on a grand scale.
French troops capture the citadel of Bắc Ninh.
UNESCO lists quan họ folk singing.
Bắc Ninh and Bắc Giang merge into one province.
Quan họ singers still perform at the spring festivals.
